Start by separating retrieval—the selection and ordering of records—from generation, which turns supplied records into prose. Chapter 1’s summary below returns to why that distinction matters.

The opening puzzles are excerpts from the book’s dated observations, not new product tests. Their answers retain the book’s uncertainty. Follow the product evidence register for sources, dates and unresolved gaps.

1. The problem5 minutes · reading and reflection

Three observations to keep open

Puzzle 1. Take a genuine question—is there an open-access citation advantage?—and append a string of invented nonsense, a word that appears in no paper anywhere. Run it in scite. Under Boolean logic, that one impossible term should empty the result list. Instead, nothing breaks: useful papers still appear near the top, and the interface still reports millions of results. Why didn’t the impossible term kill the search?

Puzzle 2. Search open access in Google Scholar and it reports about 9.4 million results. Now try to see them. The interface stops at page 100—one thousand records—and Google’s own help documentation confirms that no more than 1,000 results will ever be shown for a single query. So what are the other 9,399,000 “results”? Were they ranked? Were they even scored?

Puzzle 3. The name Semantic Scholar promises search by meaning—so a natural-language question ought to be exactly the query it handles best. It is not. In August 2026, Is there an open access citation advantage returned just 13 results, for a topic with hundreds of relevant papers. Strip the question down to its keywords—open access citation advantage—and the same system returned about 35,300. Same information need, same words at its core, a 2,700-fold difference in results. Why did the more natural query retrieve dramatically less?

Pause and reflect

For one search you know, distinguish what the screen shows from what you would need documentation to establish.

2. Foundations10 minutes · reading and reflection

Chapter 1 · The retrieval problem

What this chapter established

  1. Answer-generating academic search tools are retrieval pipelines with a writing step at the end; in the one pipeline vendors document well, four of five stages are retrieval.
  2. Retrieval and generation are separate problems. A fabricated citation is a generation failure; a missing paper may have been lost during retrieval or omitted from the answer. Inspect the working set before diagnosing.
  3. The shortlist bottleneck: retrieval limits the evidence supplied to generation. In current tools, that shortlist can be as small as five records.
  4. An LLM can sit inside the retrieval half of a pipeline; its presence says nothing about which retrieval method is being used.
  5. Tools differ along two independent axes: output format and retrieval iteration. Neither records agency.
  6. The query is a representation of the information need; matching it supplies evidence about relevance, not relevance itself. A system can estimate suitability; it cannot make the judgement.
  7. Three familiar results—a nonsense term that did not empty a result list, a reported count far larger than the viewable list, and a natural-language question that retrieved fewer papers than a shorter keyword query—leave three questions about admission, ranking and architecture open.

Explaining these puzzles—and auditing pipelines like the one that opened this chapter—requires knowing what a search system does with words before it does anything else. Chapter 2 begins with the strictest possible answer: words as admission rules.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 2 · Boolean admission and the inverted index

What this chapter established

  1. Text is not searched; analysed terms are. Tokenisation, case folding, stop-word handling and stemming all happen before anything is indexed.
  2. Query and document must be analysed compatibly. A mismatch between the two is a silent and common source of retrieval failure.
  3. An inverted index maps terms to posting lists, which is why Boolean evaluation is set intersection and union rather than a scan of documents.
  4. Boolean retrieval produces an eligible set, not an ordering. Nothing in the mechanism says which eligible record should appear first.

An eligible set of forty thousand records is not a result list anyone can use. The next chapter asks what has to be added to turn matching into ranking.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 3 · BM25 and ranked lexical retrieval

What this chapter established

  1. Ranked retrieval assigns graded scores and orders candidates; it does not specify where the scores come from. BM25 is one lexical answer.
  2. Rarer terms carry more weight, repeated terms saturate, and document length is normalised against the collection average, to a degree set by b.
  3. The index does not change. The same posting lists that answered a Boolean query support a ranked one.
  4. BM25 is a first-stage ranker in production library and scholarly systems, not a historical curiosity.

Ranking changes what a result list looks like. It also changes what happens to a query term the system cannot match at all—and that is where the central misconception of this book begins.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 4 · Lexical search beyond strict Boolean

What this chapter established

  1. Boolean-then-ranking is a common academic-search pattern, but minimum-match and direct any-match ranking are lexical too.
  2. Analysis, execution rules, query transformation — or a term that simply matched no posting list — can explain a missing typed word without implying dense or semantic retrieval. Understanding matters when its interpretation triggers one of those changes.
  3. Admission, ranking and the top-k output boundary are separate controls.
  4. Part I explains the scite and Google Scholar behaviours — and shows why the mechanism behind each is undecidable from the interface. The Semantic Scholar observation remains open until semantic capability, dense representation and pipeline stage can be separated.

Non-Boolean does not mean non-lexical. Part II next asks how a learnt representation can connect texts that share no analysed terms, then whether that mechanism is the same thing as semantic search.

Read the full explanation and evidence

What a result screen can settle

The one collapse of this kind you can catch from a result screen, which is why it is settled here rather than held over to Part II. It needs nothing a vendor had to write down—only the recognition that a result can lack a typed term for several reasons, including an admission rule other than strict all-term conjunction.

lexical search = Boolean search
A record can come back missing one of your words while the system is scoring on nothing but words. Boolean retrieval is one form of lexical retrieval; minimum-match rules and BM25 ranking can remain lexical too, and only the all-term conjunction requires every processed term. Any-match eligibility can also be expressed as Boolean OR; the separate ranking function supplies graded scores. See Lexical search does not have to mean Boolean search.

The second puzzle points the same way, though it settles into an observation rather than a confusion worth naming. A reported count is an estimate of matches, and a display limit is a display boundary rather than a scoring decision. The verdict above sets out the general form: admission decides who competes, the ranking function orders them, and the output boundary decides how many are kept—three separate controls, of which an interface reports only the last.

Neither observation required a claim about architecture, and neither yielded one: the mechanism behind each behaviour stays undecidable from the screen. That is the finding, not a shortfall.

Pause and reflect

If a result lacks one of your query words, what different mechanisms could explain it? What evidence would separate them?

3. Mechanisms15 minutes · reading and reflection

What the words on the box do not name

Five confusions are left. Part I settled a sixth by watching a system behave; none of these five can be settled that way, and none can be stated honestly before the mechanism exists. They are the same category error every time: the vocabulary of modern retrieval names goals, representations, output boundaries and whole research fields—and product descriptions use all four as though they named an architecture. Part II is where each acquires a mechanism, and the entries below link to the section that supplies it.

vector = embedding
An embedding produces a vector, but not every vector is an embedding; “embedding search” is informal and “vector embedding search” adds little precision. Read the distinction in Chapter 5.
vector search = semantic search
Vectors can be sparse, calculated and lexical; using vectors does not establish semantic matching. Read the distinction in Chapter 8.
semantic search = dense retrieval
Semantic names a goal; dense retrieval names one technical route towards it. Read the distinction in Chapter 7.
top-k belongs to dense retrieval
Top-k is an output boundary for ranked results, regardless of how their scores were produced. Read the distinction in Chapter 7.
neural information retrieval = dense retrieval
Neural IR also includes learnt sparse retrieval, late interaction and neural reranking. Read the distinction in Chapter 9.

Most of these will still mean nothing to you. Read the panel now to know what Part II is arguing about, and again at the end to see whether you can state each one in your own words. Appendix D maps the wider terminology overlaps.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 5 · Embeddings: what the learnt geometry encodes

What this chapter established

  1. A dense retriever compares learnt representations rather than strings, which is what allows it to bridge paraphrase.
  2. Context changes a token’s representation, but contextualisation alone does not decide what evidence retrieval should reward.
  3. Pretraining supplies broad language patterns; domain pretraining changes the text and vocabulary behind those patterns; neither by itself creates a retriever.
  4. A model name such as BERT therefore leaves both its task training and its place in the search pipeline unknown.

The encoder now exists, but it is not yet retrieval infrastructure. Chapter 6 turns its contextual representations into comparable query and document vectors, and asks which training examples make closeness mean relevance rather than merely linguistic similarity.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 6 · From language model to retrieval encoder

What this chapter established

  1. Contextual encoding and retrieval are separate things. A pretrained encoder supplies representations; retrieval training decides what it places close together, so every embedding space embodies an operational model of relevance shaped by its training signals.
  2. Model tokenisation and index analysis are different processes producing different units. A model token is not an indexed term.

That is an encoder, not yet a retrieval system. The next two chapters put one to work against a whole collection and then open the stored representation itself, resolving both distinctions promised in Chapter 4: semantic search is not synonymous with dense retrieval, and a vector need not be dense, learnt or semantic.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 7 · Dense retrieval at collection scale

What this chapter established

  1. Similarity is a comparison rule applied to stored vectors, not a verdict about them. Cosine similarity divides out both vector lengths and ranks on direction alone; an unnormalised dot product also responds to length, so the two rules can order the same candidates differently.
  2. A single-vector bi-encoder has to compress a passage before it knows what will be asked of it, which is why broad similarity can dominate a small but decisive detail.
  3. Approximate nearest-neighbour search often makes dense retrieval practical at large scale, and it introduces its own effects at the candidate boundary.
  4. Semantic search describes a goal rather than an architecture. BM25, ontology expansion, dense retrieval and neural reranking name mechanisms a system may combine in pursuit of it.
  5. Dense retrieval assigns similarity scores and orders candidates; top-k sets a result boundary rather than defining a retrieval method.

Both routes compared stored representations without ever asking what one of those representations contains, or what a single stored item stands for in the collection a reader believes they are searching. The next chapter opens the stored object itself.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 8 · Representations and indexed units

What this chapter established

  1. A vector is an ordered list of numbers and nothing more. Binary presence, term frequency, TF–IDF and BM25 weights can all be written as vectors, so the word names the numerical object rather than any property of it.
  2. Sparse and dense describe the shape of a representation; specified and learnt describe how the rule that produced its numbers was obtained. The two axes vary independently—BM25 is sparse with a specified rule, SPLADE is sparse with a learnt one.
  3. Density decides nothing about meaning. A fully active vector of bibliographic facts is dense and not semantic; a learnt sparse representation can be meaning-aware with almost every dimension left at zero.
  4. Source document, indexed unit, representation and result aggregation are four separate choices, and only the last of them is visible in a result list.
  5. A retrieval stage can match only its indexed evidence. A later fetch may supply more text, so indexed units and generator context must be documented separately.

A first-stage retriever, lexical or dense, has to be fast enough to run against an entire collection—which limits how carefully it can compare anything. The next chapter asks what a system can afford once it has a shortlist.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 9 · Reranking and multi-stage retrieval

What this chapter established

  1. Multi-stage retrieval exists because accuracy and scale trade against each other.
  2. A reranker can only reorder what the first stage returned. It cannot recover a document that was never retrieved.
  3. Neural information retrieval is an umbrella category, not a synonym for dense retrieval. It includes dense bi-encoders, learnt sparse retrieval, late interaction and neural reranking.
  4. Joint encoding, late interaction and learnt sparse retrieval preserve different amounts of query–document evidence and can occupy different pipeline stages.

A later stage can spend more computation, but only on candidates an earlier stage admitted. Chapter 10 turns to a different design decision: running more than one candidate-generation route, deciding whether to blend or route them, and combining ranked lists whose scores may not share a scale.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 10 · Hybrid retrieval and rank fusion

What this chapter established

  1. Hybrid retrieval is a claim about how results are combined, not merely about containing two retrievers.
  2. Blending and routing are different designs: one merges on every query, the other chooses per query.

Hybrid retrieval is not a quality guarantee. Its result depends on the evidence each route preserves, the candidate depth allowed to each, and the rule used to combine them. RRF is a useful neutral baseline because it avoids pretending unlike scores are commensurable, but its rank-only view also discards score gaps and inherits every input cut-off. Routing adds another decision: which evidence was allowed to compete at all. Chapter 11 therefore separates interpretation, transformation and routing before Chapter 12 asks who chooses the next action.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 11 · Understanding, transforming and routing queries

What this chapter established

  1. The useful question comes before phrasing: what object stands for the information need, and what mechanism will receive it?
  2. Free-text strings, controlled expressions, citation edges, seed documents, relevance judgements, browse targets, API predicates and task briefs address different mechanisms.
  3. Query understanding interprets a request and may or may not change what retrieval receives.
  4. Transformation creates changed or additional retrieval inputs; routing and coordination control which retrieval paths use them.
  5. Pseudo-relevance feedback constructs a later query from an initial ranking. It is retrieval-dependent, but a prescribed two-pass workflow need not be agentic.
  6. Query2doc and HyDE use generated text differently, which makes that text part of the search strategy and part of what must be recorded.
  7. Natural-language filter extraction is useful and reliably partial.

Interpretation, transformation, routing and feedback can all be arranged in advance. Part III asks who chooses the next action while a search is running.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 12 · Agentic search

What this chapter established

  1. Fixed, adaptive and agentic describe who decides the next action, not how documents are scored — and they are landmarks on a spectrum, not three species.
  2. Result-dependent query content does not by itself make control adaptive or agentic: two-pass PRF can sit inside a fixed sequence.
  3. An adaptive workflow may have a model choosing its branches. What makes it adaptive is constrained selection among explicitly enumerated branches; agentic control plans a trajectory from reusable actions, even though its tools are predefined too.
  4. Agency does not change the underlying retriever’s scoring function, but a loop can improve the overall search process by observing failure and choosing another action.
  5. An agent can only choose among the tools it has. Reasoning does not substitute for a missing capability, and iteration cannot invent one.
  6. A trace shows what a system did. It does not reveal what the system could have done, which is a separate and largely invisible limit.
  7. Recall failures can compound across rounds when later actions depend too narrowly on earlier results; additional routes or reformulations can also recover candidates and increase cumulative recall.
  8. Agentic RAG is a narrower case of agentic search, not a synonym for it.
  9. What the loop buys is recovery. A query that returns nothing stops being the end of the interaction and becomes the input to the next attempt — which is why an ordinary keyword search inside a loop can beat a cleverer one-shot rewrite over the same index.
  10. That recovery runs on what the open web knows. Coverage, entitlements and local quirks are what it cannot supply, and what a library can.

The pipeline is now complete, from interpreting and transforming retrieval inputs through to the controller that sequences later actions. That makes a different question possible: not what each component does, but where a particular search went wrong.

Pause and reflect

Choose a familiar product. Which retrieval stages can you document, and which are still assumptions? A label such as semantic or AI is not an answer.

4. Professional practice10 minutes · reading and reflection

Chapter 13 · Diagnosing retrieval failure

What this chapter established

  1. Vocabulary mismatch is the familiar problem of a query and relevant document expressing related concepts in different lexical forms.
  2. OOV is always relative to a specified vocabulary. A tokeniser’s ability to encode a string does not establish that the retriever has learnt a useful representation for it.
  3. OOD concerns transfer from training to deployment. In neural IR it can cover shifts in queries or corpora and, in some work, retrieval task or relevance pattern.
  4. Negation, relations and composition can fail even when vocabulary is familiar and lexical overlap is complete.
  5. These are different diagnostic lenses rather than parallel categories. They can overlap, and remedies must be tested against the suspected origin of the failure.

Diagnosis supplies hypotheses, not proof. The next chapter shows how to turn those hypotheses into comparisons—and how to decide what “better retrieval” means for the task at hand.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 14 · Measuring whether retrieval worked

What this chapter established

  1. Relevance is a relationship among information, a represented need, a person and a situation—not an intrinsic document property.
  2. Retrieval metrics measure performance against an operational definition of relevance encoded in human judgements, not objective correctness.
  3. Extending a fixed ranking cannot decrease recall, but precision can rise or fall; depth often trades screening burden against recall, and library tasks sit at opposite ends of that trade; a better system can improve both at the same depth.
  4. Within a fixed candidate set, later stages can improve ordering but cannot recover exclusions; additional retrieval routes or rounds can expand the cumulative set and increase recall.
  5. MRR, MAP and nDCG encode different definitions of a good ranking, so quoting one is choosing one.
  6. A benchmark measures performance on someone else’s topics, judged by someone else’s assessors, which is why a leaderboard position does not transfer.
  7. A local evaluation set is the one measurement whose definition of relevance the library chose, and its value lies in being rerun.

Measurement can tell a library which system to prefer. It cannot say what happened inside any particular search, or make that search repeatable a year from now. The final chapter turns to what has to be recorded, inspected and required.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Chapter 15 · Implications for library practice and tool evaluation

What this chapter established

  1. Reproducibility is conditional on a fixed system, and it is also a documentation practice rather than a property of a method.
  2. Saving the natural-language question is insufficient whenever the system rewrote it.
  3. A faithful explanation is an execution trace. A plausible narrative is not evidence of what drove a result.
  4. Documentation and inspection cannot be assumed to arrive later. A vendor may add them, but a product that was not built to expose what it searched will not do so on a library’s timetable, which is why these are procurement questions rather than support tickets.
  5. The questions that separate a retrieval design from a marketing label need no mathematics — only the distinctions this book has drawn, and the willingness to ask which one a vendor’s word names.
  6. Libraries do not need model weights. They need enough visibility to establish what was searched, enough documentation to compare it later, and enough control to test it locally.

5. Next action5 minutes · reading and reflection

The three puzzles, and what each one settled

Evidence register · 7 claim(s)

Adding an invented string left useful-looking results and a reported total in the millions.

The open access query reported about 9.4 million matches in the supplied example.

Help documentation limits display to 1,000 results for a single query.

The question returned 13 results; the unquoted keyword query returned about 35,300.

The 2025 account describes keyword retrieval over titles, abstracts and author names in Elasticsearch.

The 2025 relevance endpoint limits keyword candidates to 1,000.

The 2025 relevance endpoint reranks candidates with LightGBM.

Chapter 1 posed three ordinary search behaviours and left them open. This is where each of them ended up.

Puzzle 1 · sciteUnresolved
An invented string did not empty a result list reporting millions of matches. Analysis may have discarded the term, an upstream rewrite may have removed or changed it, the execution rule may have made it optional, or it may have been optional and matched no posting list. Matching evidence may also be outside the visible excerpt. The screen cannot separate those possibilities, and looking harder will not help. Chapter 4’s verdict.
Puzzle 2 · Google ScholarUnresolved as to ranking
About 9.4 million results reported, with a documented limit of 1,000 shown. A display limit is an output boundary: it establishes what you may page through, and nothing whatever about which signals produced the order. Chapter 4’s verdict.
Puzzle 3 · Semantic ScholarResolved as to architecture — from a document
A natural-language question returned 13 results where the keywords returned about 35,300. The vendor’s published technical account describes lexical first-stage retrieval and a learnt reranker over a capped candidate set. That settles the dense-retrieval assumption; the exact cause of the August 2026 counts remains unproven. Without that account, this one would have joined the other two. Chapter 7’s account.

Two of the three could not be settled from the interface. The third was settled — as far as a 2025 document can settle a 2026 observation — by something a vendor chose to write down.

Build a local evaluation set

If you do one thing with it, make it the evaluation set. Thirty to fifty queries out of real practice, the handful of records that ought to surface for each, judged to a fixed depth, deliberately including the searches you already know go badly. Building and judging the set takes time; an afternoon may suffice to rerun an established set, depending on the systems and judgement depth. It is also the only measurement in this book whose definition of relevance your library chose, and the only one you can rerun the next time a system changes underneath a saved search without telling anybody.

Start with one comparison using the evaluation kit’s template and worked example, then grow the set from searches that matter locally.

Read the full explanation and evidence

Choose one information need and write its relevance criteria. Which known relevant records should a good search find? Collecting and judging the runs is a separate next step.

Turn the reading into a next step

Start small with the local retrieval evaluation kit. One comparison is preparation for the longer task of constructing and judging a 30–50-query evaluation set, not a substitute for it.

For procurement, use the vendor questionnaire. For unfamiliar vocabulary, open the linked glossary. For deeper reading, keep the book’s specialist reader routes.
